title: Justification: Faith and Works
lead: Justification means being put right with God, declared or made righteous in his sight. Paul says a person is justified by faith apart from works of the law, and James says a person is justified by works and not by faith alone. How these fit together divided the Western church at the Reformation, and the churches still explain it differently.

sections.b: The Hebrew verb tsadaq and the Greek dikaioō are often used of a court that declares someone in the right: judges are to "declare the one in the right to be in the right, and the guilty one to be guilty" (Deuteronomy 25:1). "Abram put his trust in the LORD, and he reckoned it to him as righteousness" (Genesis 15:6). Psalm 32 calls blessed the one whose sin the LORD does not count (Psalm 32:1–2), and Habakkuk says the righteous will live by faith (Habakkuk 2:4). Paul builds on all three: everyone has sinned, and all are justified freely by God's grace through the redemption in Christ, received by faith (Romans 3:21–28; Romans 4:1–8; Galatians 2:16). James uses Abraham's offering of Isaac and Rahab's hiding of the spies to argue that faith without works is dead (James 2:14–26; Joshua 2:1–21).
sections.refs: Deuteronomy 25:1; Genesis 15:6; Psalm 32:1–2; Habakkuk 2:4; Romans 3:21–28; Romans 4:1–8; Galatians 2:16; James 2:14–26; Joshua 2:1–21

sections.b: Most readers think Paul and James answer different questions. Paul argues against relying on keeping the law to be accepted by God; James argues against a faith that is only words and produces no change. Paul himself says faith works through love (Galatians 5:6) and that believers are created for good works (Ephesians 2:8–10), and both Jesus and Paul say God will judge everyone by what they have done (Matthew 25:31–46; Romans 2:6–13). Since the 1970s, scholars of the "New Perspective on Paul," such as E. P. Sanders, James Dunn and N. T. Wright, have argued that Paul's "works of the law" refers mainly to the markers that set Jews apart from Gentiles, such as circumcision and food laws, rather than to good deeds in general. Others defend the older reading.
sections.refs: Galatians 5:6; Ephesians 2:8–10; Matthew 25:31–46; Romans 2:6–13; Romans 3:28; James 2:24

sections.b: Lutherans teach that sinners are justified by grace through faith alone, for Christ's sake, when God counts Christ's righteousness as theirs (Augsburg Confession 4). Reformed, Anglican and Baptist confessions agree, and add that justifying faith is never alone but always brings good works. Catholic teaching, set out at the Council of Trent, holds that justification is not only forgiveness but also the inner renewal of the person by grace poured into the heart, received in baptism, so that faith, hope and love together make a person righteous. Orthodox theology speaks less in courtroom terms and more of healing and union with God, in which faith and works belong together. Methodists teach justification by faith, followed by a lifelong growth in holiness. In 1999 Lutherans and Catholics signed a Joint Declaration stating a shared understanding of basic truths, while noting differences that remain; Methodist, Reformed and Anglican bodies later affirmed it.
sections.refs: Romans 3:24–28; Romans 5:1–5; Titus 3:5–7; Galatians 5:6; James 2:24; 2 Peter 1:4

common: Christians agree that God saves by grace, and that real faith shows itself in a changed life.
uncommon: Some New Perspective scholars hold that justification in Paul is mainly about who belongs to God's people, not how an individual is saved.
